paragraphs: In the second month, I was allowed to observe emergency medicine at a hospital in the city of Malmo. In the first week, I followed the supervising doctor and deepened my understanding of the hospital's system and cases, but from the second week I had opportunities to be in charge of actual patients. After receiving from the doctor an explanation of the chart, which recorded the past medical history and so on, and of the circumstances that led to the emergency visit, I did the interview and physical examination myself and presented the results to the senior doctor, thus experiencing the whole flow of emergency practice.

I think the biggest barrier in a clerkship is language, but personally I did not feel a language problem that hindered the clerkship. What was common to both departments was that the doctors spoke fluent English and I hardly felt any great difficulty in communication. There were also doctors equivalent to Japanese junior residents and senior residents, and I had opportunities to discuss cases with them, which was very educational. Conferences were in Swedish in many cases in either department, but even though they were busy, the doctors kindly explained in English, for which I was very grateful. As for how to deal with patients, in pediatric cardiology the patients are children, and in emergency medicine there were many elderly patients, so there were situations in which I could not understand what was going on. Even in such cases, however, the doctors explained kindly in response to my questions, which helped a lot. On the other hand, some young patients were fluent in English, and I had valuable opportunities to do interviews and physical examinations in English. Also, in both departments there were doctors who were interested in Japan, and we were able to talk about various things such as Japanese tourist spots, culture and differences in medical care. As a result, we could discuss themes that I seldom have a chance to think about in Japan, and it was a very meaningful experience.

In pediatric cardiology, I basically sat in on the outpatient clinic and learned the basic way of reading pediatric cardiac echo, how to read echo views, and the details of patients' diseases. I was also allowed to observe ward work, catheter treatment and pediatric cardiac surgery.

When discussing patients' diseases with the doctors, I made a point of comparing Japanese and European treatment guidelines and being conscious of "why was this treatment policy chosen for this patient," and I feel that I acquired a basic way of thinking about pediatric cardiology.

Also, in Sweden I often saw them actively sending genetic tests to research institutions for cases in which a family history was suspected. I realised that Sweden's own medical culture has been formed for these reasons: because medical information is managed by the personal ID given to citizens, it is easy to trace hereditary diseases and introduce tests based on family history; because the introduction of genome analysis is advancing through a national initiative called Genomics Medicine Sweden; and because public insurance coverage lowers the hurdle for genetic testing. In emergency medicine, in the first week I followed the doctors and observed interviews and physical examinations. From the second week, I was given opportunities to do the interview and physical examination as the first touch with patients who could be dealt with in English, present to the senior doctor and hand over. I experienced in person the whole flow of emergency care, going to the patient and communicating. Also, some patients came on referral from a General Practitioner, and some, before walking in to the emergency department, called a hotline to ask whether they should go to the emergency department, and I gained a lot through aspects that differ greatly from the Japanese healthcare system, such as the sorting of initial response in Swedish emergency care.

Also, Sweden has adopted a GP (General Practitioner) system like the UK's, and in large hospitals like the ones where we did our clerkships, there was little tendency to do long-term patient management. In such hospitals the treatment is mainly acute-phase, and I felt that the division of roles, in which chronic-phase management is done by the GP assigned to the patient, is made clearer than in Japan. Regarding emergency care, a team system has been introduced, and a very distinctive feature was the system in which patients whose triage had been completed were assigned to specialist teams by type of disease and each specialist emergency physician dealt with them. On the cultural side, as typified by "Fika," in Sweden there are frequent light conference-like times, even during work, gathered around coffee and bread, in which cases are consulted on and chat is mixed in. I felt that the value is deeply rooted that good ideas are born precisely in a harmonious and relaxed atmosphere rather than in a busy and tense environment.

As for housing, I stayed at lodging rented through Airbnb, the home's facilities were also well equipped, and I was able to live comfortably without inconvenience. As for cooking, I cooked using ingredients bought at a nearby supermarket. The supermarket is somewhat more expensive than in Japan, but it also sold rice and Japanese seasonings, and combined with the food I brought from Japan, I had almost no trouble with Japanese food. During my stay in Lund, I never felt any danger to my safety, and it was a very easy place to live. Beginning with Lund Cathedral, the whole town had a calm atmosphere, and I was able to visit many places during my stay. As for Malmo, although there are safety cautions such as that it is better not to walk around some areas at night, within the range where I lived I felt no danger and was able to spend my time without problems. As for the climate, in February when I arrived there were many cloudy days and the daylight hours were short, but from around March the temperature gradually rose and the days became longer, and the atmosphere changed all at once to a spring-like one. Just before returning home, the plants in the city were also beautiful and a spectacular scenery spread out, and I was able to enjoy the changing of the seasons.
